title: The Legal Ethics of Generative AI
author: Andrew M. Perlman

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source shifts attention away from direct-to-consumer access and users’ limited verification capacity toward lawyers’ court filings. It argues that broad AI-specific restrictions are unnecessary because existing procedural and ethical duties already govern false filings, supporting restrained regulation but not substantively assessing the cluster’s central risk-shifting proposition.
qs: Not only is the court order overbroad, but it is also unnecessary.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: Perlman shifts the inquiry from consumer access, UPL boundaries and provider reform to lawyers’ professional duties. He argues that existing Model Rules generally permit safeguarded use and that AI-specific judicial bans or notification requirements are unnecessary or problematic, while not addressing whether cheaper assistance improves access to justice or protects self-represented users.
qs: First, lawyers can typically use generative AI in ethically compliant ways by adopting appropriate procedures and protocols.
Second, judicial efforts to prohibit these tools or impose notification requirements are either problematic or unnecessary.

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: The source addresses court-imposed bans and disclosure duties for litigation filings, not how legal education should develop independent judgment, verification skills or professional readiness. Its criticism of broad restrictions is compatible with the cluster’s nuanced treatment of AI policy, but it does not provide enough evidence to accept or reject the cluster’s central proposition.
qs: Obligations Imposed by Court Order   Some courts have responded to the emergence of generative AI by issuing standing orders that impose near-outright bans on lawyers’ use of AI or require lawyers to disclose when they have used the technology for court filings.53 Both types of orders are overly broad and unnecessary.

st.t: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts
st.an: The source supports conditional generative-AI assistance under continuing lawyer responsibility and existing professional and procedural duties. It represents the cluster’s ordinary-rule side of the disclosure debate, arguing that broad bans and mandatory disclosure are unnecessary and difficult to delimit.
qs: As noted earlier, the rules of professional conduct and rules of civil procedure impose sufficient duties on lawyers with regard to their filings.

st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s core proposition that generative AI may be used in litigation but does not displace lawyers’ existing duties of reasonable inquiry and filing accuracy. It also supports the cluster’s distinction between settled accuracy obligations and disputed AI-specific disclosure rules, though some views are reported rather than clearly endorsed by the author.
qs: Grossman et al., Is Disclosure and Certification of the Use of Generative AI Really Necessary?, 107 JUDICATURE 69, 76 (2023) (arguing that current standing orders with disclosure requirements unnecessarily burden litigants).

st.t: Filing duties: AI use never displaces inquiry
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition by applying existing Rule 11 reasonable-inquiry and support requirements to court filings and citing sanctions for AI-generated fictitious citations. It treats AI use as subject to existing filing duties rather than as prohibited in itself, but does not materially develop the cluster’s procedural and mental-state nuances.
qs: June 22,  2023) (sanctioning attorney under FRCP 11 for submitting document with fictitious citations generated by ChatGPT).

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The source strongly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: lawyers remain accountable for AI-assisted work, must verify outputs before reliance, and can generally be governed through existing professional duties and sanctions. It takes one side of the cluster’s acknowledged policy dispute by opposing broad AI-specific bans, disclosures and certifications in favor of technology-neutral enforcement and reminders.
qs: A lawyer might reasonably decide to use a generative AI tool after considering these factors, but the lawyer should still carefully review all AI-generated content for accuracy before relying on it.
For now, the best approach is for courts to rely on their existing ability to sanction lawyers or to simply remind lawyers that they should be careful when using generative AI.

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account that professional duties continue during AI adoption and supplies one side of the dispute over regulatory adequacy: it argues that existing Model Rules accommodate careful use and that competence may eventually require AI. Its support is limited because it does not substantively address whether human accountability amounts to effective control, independent verification, or expertise preservation, and offers no measured performance evidence.
qs: First, lawyers can typically use generative AI in ethically compliant ways by adopting appropriate procedures and protocols.

The final section of this essay makes an even more provocative claim: generative AI is advancing so rapidly that we may eventually move away from saying that lawyers are ethically permitted to use it, to saying that lawyers are ethically required to do so.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The source supports safeguarded, human-accountable use of generative AI and rejects unrestricted reliance, aligning with the cluster’s copilot and risk-based adoption framing. It also reinforces the cluster’s account of disagreement over broad disclosure rules, while adding a prediction that competence duties may eventually require careful AI use. It does not directly substantiate the cluster’s central empirical claim that verification costs determine practical value.
qs: As noted earlier, the rules of professional conduct and rules of civil procedure impose sufficient duties on lawyers with regard to their filings.

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition by identifying fabricated quotations and citations as current reliability risks and treating AI use in legal briefing as permissible only through a conditional process addressing accuracy and reliability. It also aligns with reliance on existing sanctions mechanisms, though it does not assess error rates, mitigation effectiveness or verification costs empirically.
qs: On hallucinations, they make stuff up—even quotes and citations.
Any party believing a platform has the requisite accuracy and  reliability for legal briefing may move for leave and explain why.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Perlman aligns with the cluster’s core view that generative AI offers meaningful workflow benefits but presently requires careful, lawyer-supervised use rather than unrestricted autonomy. His emphasis on safeguards, existing professional duties, improving reliability and cautious near-term adoption supports selective deployment, although he does not materially examine the cluster’s apprenticeship, labour-market or pricing risks.
qs: First, lawyers can typically use generative AI in ethically compliant ways by adopting appropriate procedures and protocols.

The answer is almost certainly, “no.” As Bill Gates once said, “People often overestimate what will happen in the next two years and underestimate what will happen in ten.”75 Generative AI’s potential to transform the legal profession is enormous, but it will not lead to seismic changes in the immediate future.

st.t: Litigation responsibility: Sanctions follow conduct and authority
st.an: The source supports continuing human accountability for court filings by grounding responsibility in Rule 11(b)’s reasonable-inquiry and evidentiary-support requirements and citing Mata as a concrete sanction for fictitious ChatGPT-generated citations. It does not materially develop the cluster’s broader account of drafting-chain responsibility, remediation, or context-dependent sanctions.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: Perlman accepts the cluster’s core supervised-AI model: lawyers may use generative AI only with tool- and task-sensitive oversight, accuracy review, confidentiality safeguards and continuing professional accountability. He is more optimistic that safeguarded use can retain value and eventually become professionally required, but does not dispute the present need for substantive verification or lifecycle scrutiny.
qs: A lawyer might reasonably decide to use a generative AI tool after considering these factors, but the lawyer should still carefully review all AI-generated content for accuracy before relying on it.

st.t: Supervisory accountability: Verification must test substantive support
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI does not displace lawyers’ professional responsibility and that outputs require careful human review before reliance. It also supports proportionate, risk-sensitive safeguards rather than a categorical prohibition, although it does not materially develop the cluster’s institutional-leadership accountability or source-level substantive-verification framework.

st.an: The source supports selective, human-supervised deployment: lawyers should assess benefits and risks by context, apply greater oversight to more sophisticated uses, and verify AI output before reliance. kp.k: Existing ethics rules accommodate careful generative AI use
kp.d: Perlman argues that the ABA Model Rules provide an adaptable framework rather than a regulatory barrier to lawyers’ use of generative AI. Drawing on the Ethics 20/20 Commission’s technology-related amendments, he maintains that appropriate safeguards and procedures permit many uses, while explicitly acknowledging that the essay does not address every ethical issue or application.
qs: the overarching point is that lawyers can use these tools in many contexts if they employ appropriate safeguards and procedures.
The Model Rules offer an adaptable framework for guiding lawyers on their use of generative AI.

kp.k: Confidentiality requires provider scrutiny and appropriate safeguards
kp.d: Perlman interprets Rules 1.6 and 5.3 as requiring reasonable efforts to protect client information, analogous to existing obligations for cloud storage, email and legal research services. He cautions against entering confidential information into most public generative AI services without informed consent because providers may review prompts or use them for training. He regards ChatGPT Enterprise’s protections as likely sufficient, not categorically guaranteed; the accompanying footnote acknowledges access by authorized employees and contractors subject to confidentiality and security obligations. Provider reputation, location and contractual terms also matter.
qs: These issues, however, are not especially novel.

This prescription means that, in the absence of informed client consent, lawyers should not insert or upload confidential information into most publicly available versions of generative AI services (like ChatGPT) because the companies operating those services typically have the right to review the prompts that are used.
For example, OpenAI has a version of ChatGPT (ChatGPT Enterprise) that includes data protection procedures that likely satisfy a lawyer’s duty of confidentiality.

kp.k: Confidentiality alternatives include generic prompts, internal tools and consent
kp.d: Alternatives to purchasing a suitably protected service include avoiding disclosure of client confidences, building an internal tool, or obtaining informed consent under Rule 1.6(a). Perlman stresses that consent requires an adequate explanation of risks and alternatives, tailored to client sophistication, and may sometimes be unattainable given limited technological understanding. As evidence that internal deployment may be affordable, he cites Gunderson Dettmer’s innovation officer’s projection that providing ChatGD firmwide would cost less than $10,000 annually; this is a reported projection, not an independently established general cost.
qs: Generative AI can be quite useful even without disclosing confidential information, just as legal research tools can be helpful without disclosing client confidences.
Second, lawyers could build their own generative AI tools.

That said, given the current lack of technological sophistication of most lawyers and clients, it may not be possible in some instances to obtain informed consent to share sensitive information with many generative AI tools.

kp.k: Client consultation is advisable, but its necessity remains uncertain
kp.d: Perlman argues that Rule 1.4(a)(2) may require consultation about substantive AI use even when confidentiality protections are adequate. He distinguishes this arguable duty from a settled universal requirement: basic autocomplete does not warrant consultation, and carefully reviewed substantive work could arguably resemble ordinary research-tool use. Nevertheless, he recommends consultation for more than minimal drafting assistance in the present environment, predicting that widespread adoption may eventually make it unnecessary.
qs: Such a consultation is only arguable because it is not entirely clear that a lawyer’s use of generative AI is sufficiently important to warrant a consultation in all circumstances.
That said, at least for now, lawyers are well-advised to consult with clients before using generative AI to assist with anything other than the de minimis case of autocompleting simple text.
Even if a duty of consultation currently exists under Rule 1.4, generative AI tools are likely to become so ubiquitous in the years to come that consultation is likely to become unnecessary.

kp.k: Oversight scales with risk; human verification remains essential
kp.d: Perlman explains that Rule 5.3 covers nonhuman assistance, reflecting its 2012 title change from “Assistants” to “Assistance.” Basic autocomplete generally needs no additional oversight, whereas sophisticated tools require consideration of training, accuracy procedures, reputation and confidentiality. Even after selecting a service, lawyers should verify all generated content before relying on it. He analogizes this responsibility to checking paralegal or summer-associate work: error risk requires closer review rather than necessarily prohibiting use.
qs: In contrast, if a lawyer uses more sophisticated forms of generative AI, there will be additional oversight obligations.
A lawyer might reasonably decide to use a generative AI tool after considering these factors, but the lawyer should still carefully review all AI-generated content for accuracy before relying on it.
A high probability of error does not mean a lawyer is prohibited from using a particular service; it just means that the lawyer must vet the content more carefully.

kp.k: Competence requires understanding both technological benefits and risks
kp.d: Perlman interprets Rule 1.1 Comment 8 as requiring ongoing awareness and assessment of generative AI’s advantages and risks, while permitting lawyers to conclude that a particular use is not worthwhile. He also flags, without comprehensively analyzing, unauthorized practice, prospective-client duties under Rule 1.18, fees under Rule 1.5 and possible mandatory training. His fee discussion specifically preserves the prohibition on billing for time not spent; it does not establish a new pricing model.
qs: In the context of generative AI, this obligation means that lawyers should understand the potential advantages and risks from the tools.
Lawyers can quite reasonably conclude that, under some circumstances, generative AI does not present a sufficient benefit to outweigh the risks and vice versa.
the prohibition against lawyers billing for time that they did not spend on a matter

kp.k: Broad judicial AI bans are unnecessary and overinclusive
kp.d: Perlman criticizes Judge Michael J. Newman’s standing order, which prohibits AI use in preparing filings while exempting specified search engines. He argues its breadth could capture ordinary productivity software and AI-assisted e-discovery. He maintains that Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 and professional-conduct obligations already provide sufficient sanctions for inaccurate filings, citing Mata v. Avianca as an actual enforcement example rather than evidence of a measured model error rate.
qs: First, by prohibiting the use of nearly all forms of AI—and not just generative AI—the order is dramatically overbroad.
Lawyers are already subject to sanctions or discipline for filing inaccurate or false documents using AI.
These provisions were more than adequate to discipline and sanction the infamous New York lawyer who cut and pasted bogus citations from ChatGPT into a court document.

kp.k: AI disclosure mandates create unnecessary boundary problems
kp.d: Perlman regards disclosure and certification requirements as preferable to bans but still overly broad. His examples include Judge Fuentes’s disclosure order and a Fifth Circuit amendment identified in the footnotes as proposed on December 1, 2023. He argues that embedded autocomplete and brainstorming make disclosure boundaries difficult to draw, while existing responsibility for filings already requires appropriate review. He rejects Judge Starr’s reasoning for additional certification through an analogy to supervised summer associates and recommends reminders or existing sanctions instead.
qs: One problem is that lawyers are now using generative AI without even realizing it.
Another problem with these orders is that they would require lawyers to disclose when they have used generative AI just to brainstorm ideas.
For now, the best approach is for courts to rely on their existing ability to sanction lawyers or to simply remind lawyers that they should be careful when using generative AI.

kp.k: AI already assists diverse drafting and analytical tasks
kp.d: Perlman reports emerging uses in transactional drafting, document summarization, emails, argument brainstorming, discovery requests, simple motions and briefs, legal memoranda, deposition preparation and identifying inconsistencies in testimony. He supports the discussion with practitioner and vendor examples, including Sullivan & Cromwell and Casetext, rather than quantified productivity studies. He presents these as assistance improving quality or efficiency within approximately one year of ChatGPT’s release, not demonstrated autonomous replacement of lawyers.
qs: Lawyers already have begun to use these tools to improve the quality of their work or make it more efficient.
These use cases have emerged within only one year of ChatGPT’s release, when these tools are in their relative infancy.

kp.k: Competence may eventually require AI adoption
kp.d: Perlman’s central forward-looking claim is that generative AI may become indispensable enough that competent practice requires its use, including starting legal drafts with AI rather than from a blank screen. He explicitly rejects an imminent transformation, citing evolving reliability, emerging use cases and cautious deployment by firms, legal departments and service providers. The prediction rests on technological expectations and analogies to email, online research and the Gartner hype cycle, not an established present obligation or a fixed adoption deadline.
qs: generative AI is advancing so rapidly that we may eventually move away from saying that lawyers are ethically permitted to use it, to saying that lawyers are ethically required to do so.
Generative AI’s potential to transform the legal profession is enormous, but it will not lead to seismic changes in the immediate future.
Competent lawyers are now expected to know how to use those tools, and the same will eventually be true for generative AI

kp.k: Access to justice is a prospective public benefit
kp.d: Perlman links possible future AI adoption to lawyers’ responsibility for the quality of justice and to unmet public legal needs, separately from efficiencies for existing clients. He presents access-to-justice improvement as a possibility, not a demonstrated outcome. Supporting references include a World Justice Project ranking described in the footnote as placing the United States 115 out of 140 countries in access to civil justice and commentary on low-cost AI legal assistance.
qs: We may even come to see generative AI as an important way to serve the public’s unmet legal needs and as a powerful tool for addressing the access-to-justice crisis.
If we take this obligation seriously, we necessarily need to consider how new technologies can help us to better serve our clients and the public.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Perlman argues that generative AI can already be used ethically to improve legal work and predicts that its eventual importance may turn use into a professional competence obligation.
pts.d: Perlman identifies current applications in drafting clauses, emails, simple transactional documents, motions, briefs and legal memoranda; summarising document collections; brainstorming arguments; preparing discovery and depositions; and identifying inconsistencies in testimony. He argues that existing Model Rules accommodate careful use rather than obstruct adoption. Confidentiality safeguards, appropriate client consultation and human verification remain necessary. He predicts increasingly ubiquitous and sophisticated tools, potentially making drafting from a blank screen professionally questionable. He also predicts that client consultation about AI use may become unnecessary as the technology becomes commonplace. He characterises broad judicial bans and disclosure requirements as unnecessary and increasingly confusing, because existing professional and procedural duties already address inaccurate filings. Finally, he suggests AI could help address unmet legal needs; this is presented as a possibility rather than a demonstrated outcome.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The argument rests principally on professional-rule interpretation, Perlman’s rule-reform experience, historical technology analogies and reported use cases—not measured productivity or performance results.
pts.d: Perlman draws on his role as Chief Reporter of the ABA Commission on Ethics 20/20 and interprets Model Rules 1.1, 1.4, 1.6 and 5.3 and their comments. He cites state ethics guidance and analogies to cloud storage, online research, email and supervision of junior personnel. Mata v. Avianca supplies a sanctions example supporting his argument that existing rules can address fabricated citations, not a measured hallucination rate. Reported Sullivan & Cromwell applications and Casetext materials support the examples of current uses. A Gunderson Dettmer report supplies its innovation officer’s projected annual ChatGD cost of less than $10,000, supporting Perlman’s suggestion that internal deployment may cost less than lawyers expect; it is not a general cost estimate. A cited Bloomberg Law survey of 452 attorneys reports almost 70% believing ethical use is possible and 66% believing use need not violate the Model Rules or state equivalents; these are attitudes, not findings of compliance. His eventual mandatory-use prediction relies on technology trajectories, the Gartner hype cycle and email’s progression from ethical concern to routine professional requirement. The access-to-justice discussion cites a World Justice Project ranking and commentary on low-cost AI assistance, without demonstrating AI-driven reductions in unmet need.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The February 2024 essay distinguishes present, conditional ethical use from a longer-term prediction of ubiquity and required competence, expressly rejecting immediate seismic change.
pts.d: Perlman supplies no fixed date for an obligation to use AI. His prediction depends on tools becoming more reliable, useful and integral to effective practice, while firms and departments remain cautious in the near term. For current use, lawyers must assess benefits and risks, protect client information and verify generated content before relying on it. Confidentiality routes include generic prompts without client confidences, appropriately protected third-party services, proprietary tools or informed consent where meaningful consent is possible. He notes that limited technological sophistication can make consent unobtainable in some situations. He recommends consultation for substantive AI use for now, while acknowledging uncertainty about whether Rule 1.4 always requires it. Oversight varies with the task and service: simple autocomplete needs little additional action, whereas substantive generation requires greater scrutiny. His interpretation concerns the Model Rules as an adaptable framework, not a claim that every jurisdiction has adopted identical requirements.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed changes affect practising lawyers, firms, in-house departments, clients, courts and people with unmet legal needs.
pts.d: Transactional lawyers and litigators gain assistance with drafting, research-related work, document analysis and preparation, while retaining responsibility for accuracy and confidentiality. Firms and legal departments face deployment, provider-selection and oversight decisions; Perlman notes that few currently have sufficient resources to build their own tools independently, although internal deployment may become more cost-effective. Clients may receive more efficient or higher-quality work but also face confidentiality risks and decisions about consent or consultation. Courts, counsel and self-represented litigants are affected by AI-specific bans and disclosure rules, which Perlman argues impose unnecessary burdens or confusion. Practising lawyers and law students may face future training expectations, and lawyers may eventually need AI proficiency to practise competently. The public with unmet legal needs is the beneficiary of his prospective access-to-justice claim. He does not predict quantified job losses, altered staffing ratios or a specific shift in provider market shares.
